name: Nevada

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Nevada became the 36th state on October 31, 1864. Congress gave it 1 seat in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, Nevada kept 1 seat in the House. It elected its one member statewide (at-large).

events.title: 1880 census apportionment

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Nevada's House delegation grew from 1 to 2 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Nevada kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Nevada's House delegation grew from 2 to 3 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Court-drawn map after two vetoes
events.text: The governor vetoed two congressional plans in May 2011. In Guy v. Miller, a Carson City court used three special masters and adopted a slightly modified version of their four-district plan on October 27, 2011.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Nevada's House delegation grew from 3 to 4 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Legislature redraws in special session
events.text: After the 2020 census, the legislature passed new congressional districts (SB 1) on November 16, 2021, and the governor signed them the same day.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Nevada kept 4 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Commission initiative kept off ballot
events.text: In Fair Maps Nevada v. Jeng, the Nevada Supreme Court upheld blocking two initiatives that would have had a seven-member commission draw congressional and legislative districts. It found they required spending without a revenue source, as the state constitution forbids.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which raised Nevada's seats from 1 to 2. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which left Nevada with 2 seats. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which raised Nevada's seats from 2 to 3. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c113.text: New map following: Court-drawn map after two vetoes. The governor vetoed two congressional plans in May 2011. In Guy v. Miller, a Carson City court used three special masters and adopted a slightly modified version of their four-district plan on October 27, 2011.
